jobs.text: For an education team building a document Q&A assistant, the closest prior work is an education voice-intent classifier delivered in 2025 [E1]. That project used Airflow for nightly DAGs that retrained and published an NLP classification model over noisy support tickets [E2]. A media fraud scorer applied a similar NLP and nightly DAG pattern, with Docker used for containerisation [E5]. For retrieval and question answering, I have built a RAG pipeline in a fintech project that also included a computer vision model [E4]. A media contract summariser used Pinecone for a managed similarity-search index with metadata filters, which maps directly to document Q&A retrieval [E6]. Computer vision is further evidenced in a travel churn predictor [E3]. The individual components are present in completed work, and the education-domain text experience is direct [E1][E2].

For a logistics recommendation engine, the key technical risk is keeping retraining and inference orchestration reliable as data changes, and that is where my adjacent-industry work is strongest. I do not have a logistics client in my project history; logistics domain experience is not a core strength I can evidence. In an energy voice-intent classifier, I used LangChain to chain prompts, tools, and output parsers, and nightly DAGs to retrain and publish an XGBoost model, improving the client's key metric by 15 percent [E1][E2]. In an education support-ticket classifier, I scheduled NLP work with Airflow and orchestrated it with LangChain, improving that client's key metric by 9 percent [E3][E4].

My cited work includes FastAPI endpoints for demand predictions and document Q&A [E1][E2][E3], and RAG pipelines for media and real estate clients [E3][E4]. Defect detection on factory-line camera frames appears in a real estate project delivered in 2025, deployed on AWS SageMaker [E4]. However, the defect detection component in [E4] is directly relevant to camera-frame inspection. On SageMaker, I have deployed models for travel and real estate clients [E1][E4]. RAG work includes building retrieval pipelines and grounding answers in retrieved passages [E3][E4][E6].

Your churn predictor for manufacturing teams needs reproducible delivery, scheduled retraining, and model serving. I built an education churn predictor with Docker, managing training jobs and endpoints in the client’s cloud account and shipping reproducible images to the client’s cluster [E1]. I do not have a manufacturing client in my supporting materials, so that specific domain is not a core strength [E1]. For FastAPI, I served travel demand and document Q&A models through FastAPI [E3][E4]. For Airflow, I built nightly DAGs that retrain and publish an education voice-intent classifier [E5][E6]. For LoRA fine-tuning, my closest evidence is parameter-efficient adapters on a 7b model in a travel demand forecaster, not explicit LoRA [E4].

For your education team’s document Q&A assistant, the relevant prior work is a RAG pipeline with MLflow run tracking and a text classification system over noisy support tickets [E1]. I have no documented education-client project, so I would treat that media engagement as the closest transferable case rather than a direct match. For a real estate client, I built a RAG pipeline and an NLP classification system, deployed on AWS SageMaker [E3].

I have documented experience with each tool, though not with a retail client directly. For Airflow, I scheduled nightly DAGs that retrained and published an NLP classifier for an education client [E1][E2]. For Pinecone and SageMaker together, I built a contract summariser for a media client, using a similarity-search index with metadata filters and pipelines on SageMaker [E3]. I have also used Pinecone for a real estate document Q&A assistant [E4] and SageMaker for managed training jobs and endpoints in an energy project [E5][E6]. I have not done contract summarisation for a retail client; that specific industry experience is not a core strength I can document. The closest match is the media contract summariser, which indicates the same retrieval and SageMaker inference approach can be applied if your retail contracts have similar text structure. I would want to confirm your data format and contract types before proposing a detailed setup.
I can support both requirements, with a caveat: my documented case studies do not include

I have built Django backends for an education admin dashboard and a retail order-tracking app, including server-rendered pages and typed interfaces [E1][E2]. For Tailwind, I have styled a real estate client portal and a logistics inventory tracker with utility-class design and responsive breakpoints [E4][E5][E6].

For Redis, I used caching in a fintech order-tracking app with websockets live updates that produced a 12% improvement in the client's key metric [E1]. For Celery, I implemented workers in a retail inventory tracker alongside Redis caching, GraphQL API, and Playwright tests, resulting in a 45% improvement [E3]; I also used Celery with Django for background email and report generation in a travel admin dashboard [E4]. For OAuth, I built login with token refresh and scopes in an energy marketplace storefront and a logistics inventory tracker [E2][E5][E6]. The logistics and retail inventory work is the closest analogue to manufacturing operations: third-party sign-in, real-time order status, and inventory tracking. I would apply that same pattern to your portal without claiming manufacturing-specific history I do not have.

For a retail client portal, the closest cited work is a real estate client portal using WebSockets live updates, typed front and back ends, Docker deployment, and Stripe payments [E3][E5]. My AWS work includes an appointment scheduler with load balancer, managed database, CDN, background task queue for emails and reports, and a single typed query endpoint replacing many REST calls [E1][E2]. WebSockets live updates also appear in a healthcare marketplace storefront that pushed real-time order status to open browsers [E4]; that order-status pattern maps to retail order tracking or inventory alerts. I implemented Stripe payments in both a real estate client portal and a travel marketplace storefront, the latter also including OAuth login, Docker deployment, caching, and rate limiting [E5][E6]. The client industries in evidence are real estate, healthcare, and travel, not retail, but the portal, checkout, and order-status flows would transfer.

Your healthcare learning portal will need secure authentication, dependable background processing, server-rendered pages, and real-time updates. I can bring those specific technical components from prior work. For background tasks, I have used Celery with Redis caching in a retail inventory tracker [E1] and Celery with Django for automated email and report generation in a travel admin dashboard [E2]; these patterns fit training reminders and completion reports. For secure access and real-time communication, I implemented OAuth sign-in with token refresh and scopes in a logistics inventory tracker [E3], and built a Node.js API with OAuth login and real-time push of order status to open browsers for a logistics client [E4]. I also built a Next.js booking platform with server-rendered pages and OAuth [E6]. These are directly relevant to portal logins, live learner dashboards, and server-rendered course content. My submitted record does not include a healthcare client specifically, so I will not claim that domain experience. However, the security-conscious patterns in these logistics, retail, and travel systems transfer to healthcare learning portal requirements.

I can show those from recent work: a retail booking platform with PostgreSQL delivered a 31% improvement in the client's key metric [E4], a logistics tracker used a Node.js API and delivered a 36% improvement in the client's key metric [E5], and a retail inventory tracker included a Playwright end-to-end regression suite in CI [E1][E2]. I also have no direct travel-client case study in my evidence; the closest comparable example is the retail booking platform cited above [E4]. I would start with the data model and API surface where I have evidence, and be transparent about the infrastructure gaps rather than overstate them.

My travel finance close model used SQL window functions and CTEs over multi-million-row tables for monthly revenue projections and backtests, replacing a manual weekly reporting routine [E1]. For pricing work, I built a healthcare pricing analysis in dbt with serverless warehouse queries and Power BI reporting, improving the client's key metric by 12% [E5]. I have designed randomized experiments with significance and power checks in BigQuery, which is the core of reliable A/B testing for fare or discount changes [E4]. I also have BigQuery deduplication and orchestration experience with Airflow [E3].

My project history is not in fintech, so I won’t claim that as a core strength. However, the relevant tools and methods appear in adjacent supply-chain work. In a retail warehouse migration delivered in 2024, I built Power BI reports and forecasting models on BigQuery, with dependency-aware nightly pipeline schedules [E2]. The work involved statistical analysis and improved the client’s key metric by 20% [E2]. That assignment required handling warehouse data, which overlaps with supply-chain analysis. A separate travel finance close model used forecasting, advanced SQL, and Python automation to achieve a 41% improvement in the client’s key metric [E3]. Manufacturing KPI reporting also involved Power BI and data deduplication across customer records, yielding 36% improvement [E1].

My manufacturing KPI reporting suite used Looker explores, Airflow orchestration, and deduplication of inconsistent customer records, with a 36% improvement in the client's key metric [E1]. My Tableau work includes a media customer segmentation study with Tableau dashboards, data cleaning, and Python automation, producing a 41% improvement [E3]. The Tableau repository also documents interactive executive dashboards with drill-downs and record deduplication [E4]. Direct logistics client work is not present in the available evidence, so I would not call logistics a core strength. The closest comparable project is the manufacturing KPI reporting suite, which addressed operational reporting and data consistency rather than a finance close model [E1]. No past finance close model is documented in the evidence.

For your education team’s marketing attribution report, the closest prior work is an education survey analysis that used hypothesis tests, confidence intervals, regression diagnostics, and Python dataframe wrangling, joining, and reshaping [E3]. That project replaced a manual weekly reporting routine for an education client and delivered a 37% improvement in the client’s key metric [E4]. I have built Airflow pipelines for healthcare survey analysis and an energy KPI reporting suite, including dependency-aware nightly schedules and statistical modelling [E1][E2]. My data cleaning experience comes from a media customer segmentation study where I handled deduplication and inconsistent customer records [E6]; that work also included randomised experiment design with significance and power checks [E5].

That work improved the client's key metric by 38% [E2]. For orchestration, I have built dependency-aware nightly pipeline schedules in Airflow, with window functions and CTEs over multi-million-row tables [E5]. I also have a tested ETL transformation layer that consolidates five source systems [E1], the kind of reconciliation often needed when moving an education team's warehouse.
